Overview

This report documents our team's participation as SST (Shanghai Senior Tour) in the grand finals of the Robbyant Embodied AI Challenge, covering model tuning, experimental analysis, and reflections after the competition.

This report has three goals:

  1. Document our participation. The challenge starts from the pretrained LingBot-VLA 2.0 6B weights, with post-training on RoboTwin demo_clean-50 and evaluation under the demo_clean and demo_randomized configurations. We document our experiments, results, and decisions along the way.
  2. Examine practical considerations in VLA SFT. We use this opportunity to explore multiple visual inputs, MetaQuery supervision, learning-rate optimization, padded actions, and related issues, and reflect on the design and training choices that matter in practice.
  3. Connect System 1 and System 2 through visual prompts. Our approach uses Qwen-SAM to provide explicit visual prompts to LingBot-VLA 2.0, turning high-level semantic understanding into foreground cues that the action model can read directly. This offers a practical direction for combining System 1 and System 2.

Model and experimental setup

We fine-tune LingBot-VLA 2.0 on RoboTwin with supervised learning, focusing on generalization from clean training data to randomized scenes.

Training dataClean-50

Clean demonstrations only
50 manipulation tasks

Global batch1,024

Micro batch 32

Action chunk50 steps

Absolute joint
Execute the full chunk by default

OptimizerMuon

Base LR 1e−4 → 5e−5
Cosine · 50k schedule

LingBot-VLA 2.0 uses a Qwen3-VL-4B backbone with three camera views, language, and a flow-matching action expert. During training, learnable queries align with frozen depth and video teachers. Inference runs only the policy, without the teachers.

We evaluate all 50 tasks in both Clean and Randomized scenes. Most ablations use 50 episodes per task; the baseline and final model use 100. Training steps and evaluation counts are shown in each table. Success rates are aggregated across all tasks, and differences are expressed in percentage points (pp).

Experiments and analysis

We first compare action representations and visual inputs, then adjust distillation and optimization, and finally revisit the training supervision itself.

01

Baseline: the Clean–Randomized gap

Starting point
Pretrained LingBot-VLA 2.0
Change
Supervised fine-tuning on RoboTwin clean-50 with absolute joint actions.

We begin with the LingBot-VLA 2.0 post-training recipe, fine-tune on clean data, and evaluate in both Clean and Randomized scenes. The model already completes most tasks in familiar scenes, but changes to backgrounds, lighting, and distractors substantially reduce its success rate.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Absolute joint15k10077.136.2
Absolute joint20k5079.633.6

At 15k, success reaches 77.1% in Clean scenes but only 36.2% in Randomized scenes. Training to 20k raises Clean to 79.6% without improving Randomized performance. This shifts our focus to inputs and supervision: how can we make learned manipulation skills less sensitive to scene appearance?

TakeawaySimply extending training on clean data does not close the generalization gap we observe.

01.a

Action space: joint outperforms end-effector

Starting point
N0 · Three original camera views
Change
Compare absolute versus relative actions, and joint versus end-effector representations.

Before changing visual inputs, we check whether the action representation limits performance. All four experiments use the same training steps and evaluation counts.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Absolute joint15k10077.136.2
Relative joint15k10077.036.7
Absolute EE15k10076.627.4
Relative EE15k10074.024.1

Joint representations clearly outperform end-effector (EE) representations in Randomized scenes, while absolute and relative joint actions perform very similarly. We therefore retain absolute joint actions and focus subsequent experiments on visual generalization.

TakeawayUse absolute joint actions in all subsequent experiments.

02

Foreground masks: dim the background, highlight the objects

Starting point
N0 · Three original camera views
Change
Use Qwen + SAM3 to identify task-relevant foreground regions and replace the main camera image.

Our first hypothesis is that appearance differences between clean and randomized scenes distract the model from the objects it needs to manipulate. Highlighting the task-relevant foreground may help it reuse the manipulation skills it has already learned.

Qwen proposes target objects from the instruction and image, and SAM3 generates segmentation masks. We preserve the foreground, multiply background pixels by 0.2, and replace the main camera image, cam_high, with the processed image. Both wrist views remain unchanged. The same foreground processing is used during training and inference.

We also compare two episode–instruction pairing strategies. Single follows the default one-to-one pairing between episodes and instructions in the LeRobot dataset, generating SAM masks for each episode using its paired instruction.

Multi instead generates SAM masks for each episode using 100 seen instructions to obtain a SAM image sequence for every instruction. During training, we randomly select one SAM-image–instruction pair and feed the current SAM frame and its corresponding instruction into the VLA.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Original images · N015k10077.136.2
SAM single15k5076.645.1
SAM multi · N115k5078.047.8
SAM multi20k5079.847.5

At 15k, multi raises Randomized success from 36.2% to 47.8%, a gain of 11.6 percentage points, with a small improvement in Clean as well. This is the largest single gain in our experiments. Multi adds another 2.7 points over single, so subsequent experiments continue to randomly sample paired SAM images and instructions.

TakeawayDirectly processing the main camera input substantially improves performance in randomized scenes.

02.a

Action chunks: the best execution length depends on the task

Starting point
N1 · The same 20k checkpoint
Change
Keep the prediction horizon at 50 steps; execute the first 50, 25, or 10 steps per cycle.

Does more frequent observation and replanning improve closed-loop control? We keep the model weights fixed and vary only the number of actions executed from each predicted chunk.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Execute 50 steps20k5079.847.5
Execute 25 steps20k5078.545.8
Execute 10 steps20k5068.523.4

Overall, executing 25 steps slightly reduces performance; shortening the execution length to 10 steps lowers Randomized success to 23.4%. This trend does not hold for every task. Each task has its own best execution length, which can also change between scenes.

Per-task comparison

Selected tasks are shown below for all three execution lengths, with 50 evaluation episodes per setting. Bold values mark the best result in each row.

TaskScene50 steps (%)25 steps (%)10 steps (%)Best length
blocks_ranking_sizeClean42628010 steps
pick_dual_bottlesRandomized60708410 steps
blocks_ranking_sizeRandomized42582025 steps
stack_blocks_twoRandomized82924025 steps
open_microwaveClean8444850 steps
place_container_plateRandomized82761650 steps

For example, blocks_ranking_size benefits from executing 10 steps in Clean scenes: success rises from 42% at 50 steps to 80%. In Randomized scenes, however, 25 steps is best at 58%, while 10 steps achieves only 20%. In Randomized scenes, pick_dual_bottles also benefits from a shorter execution length, improving from 60% at 50 steps to 84% at 10 steps.

Conversely, open_microwave achieves 84% in Clean scenes with 50 steps but only 8% with 10. More frequent replanning does not always improve success; execution length should be chosen for the task and scene. Among the 10-, 25-, and 50-step settings tested here, 50 steps gives the best overall result when using a single configuration for all tasks, so we retain it for subsequent mainline experiments.

TakeawayThe best execution length depends on both the task and the scene. With one shared configuration, 50 steps remains best overall in these experiments.

03

Mask review: improve the foreground, retain some background

Starting point
N1 · SAM multi
Change
Add VLM-based mask review, set background brightness to ×0.1, and add a 2px outline.

The initial masks sometimes miss relevant objects or include incorrect regions. We broaden candidate-object recall, then send the image, candidate masks, and object names back to Qwen to reject incorrect masks. We also reduce background brightness to 0.1 of the original image and add a 2px outline.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
SAM multi · N115k5078.047.8
Reviewed + background ×0.1 · N215k5076.050.8
Reviewed + black background15k5071.146.0

With these changes, Randomized success rises from 47.8% to 50.8%, while Clean falls from 78.0% to 76.0%. Making the background fully black worsens both results. Context outside the foreground still matters: moderate dimming works better for the current model than complete removal.

This experiment changes mask review and rendering together; the +3.0 pp gain reflects their combined effect.

TakeawayKeep reviewed multi-mask inputs, 0.1× background brightness, and outlines.

03.a

A fourth view: see both the original and SAM images

Starting point
N0 · Three original camera views
Change
Retain the original main camera image and add the SAM image in a fourth image slot.

Starting from N0 and its three original camera views, we retain the main camera image and append a SAM foreground image. Unlike N2, which replaces the main view, this gives the model access to both the original image and foreground information. We therefore compare against both the original-image baseline N0 and the input-replacement approach N2.

We compare three positional encodings: native assigns new positions to the fourth image; copy reuses the main view's (t, h, w); and copy_t1 reuses spatial positions while incrementing the temporal position. We test both the original causal mask and a pair mask. The latter makes the entire “raw-image Query → SAM Key” block visible, while attention within each view remains lower-triangular.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Original images · N015k10077.136.2
Main-view replacement · N215k5076.050.8
native / causal15k5079.241.3
copy / causal15k5077.941.8
copy_t1 / causal15k5078.542.6
native / pair15k5077.038.8
copy / pair15k5077.638.6
copy_t1 / pair15k50—37.6

With causal attention, Randomized success across the three positional encodings is 41.3%–42.6%, or 5.1–6.4 points above N0's 36.2%. Adding SAM information at the input therefore helps. However, all three remain below N2's 50.8%: for these tasks, directly suppressing background distractions is more effective than retaining the original image and appending a foreground cue.

Positional encoding is not the main driver in these experiments. Under causal attention, the three positional schemes differ by only about 1.3 points. Reusing spatial positions or explicitly separating temporal positions offers no clear advantage. By contrast, changing causal to pair with the same positional encoding reduces success by 2.6, 3.2, and 5.0 points, respectively—a consistent direction across all three schemes.

New information should be integrated in a way that preserves the VLM's native attention pattern. Causal attention retains the token-visibility relationships used during pretraining. Although pair enables more information exchange between the original and SAM images, it also changes those relationships and performs worse. Matching native attention deserves priority over designing more elaborate positional encodings.

TakeawayWhen adding visual inputs, preserving the VLM's native causal attention matters more than the positional encoding. Directly replacing the main view remains the best approach here.

03.b

MetaQuery: masks as auxiliary supervision

Starting point
N0 · Three original camera views
Change
Add learnable queries before the depth/video queries to predict the main-view mask.

This experiment also starts from N0, retaining all original image inputs and introducing SAM information through auxiliary MetaQuery supervision. Learnable queries read image and language tokens under causal attention, then predict reviewed masks through a MaskFormer-style dot product. The action expert can also read these queries. We include both N0 and N2 below to compare auxiliary supervision with direct input processing.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Original images · N015k10077.136.2
Main-view replacement · N215k5076.050.8
SAM MetaQuery15k50—37.9

MetaQuery reaches a Randomized success rate of 37.9%, 1.7 points above N0 but 12.9 points below N2. It also trails the causal fourth-view approach in 03.a by 3.4–4.7 points.

Both approaches aim to add foreground information to the VLA, but introduce it at different points. The input-side approach supplies a SAM image at inference so the VLM can directly read the extra visual information. MetaQuery instead uses a training-time mask-reconstruction objective to shape auxiliary representations. The additional supervision does not translate into a comparable improvement in manipulation success.

Taken together, these experiments favor adding new information directly at the input while preserving the VLM's native attention pattern. In our setting, replacing the main view works best, adding a fourth view with causal attention comes next, and auxiliary MetaQuery supervision provides a smaller gain. The input-side approaches require SAM image generation at inference as well.

TakeawayForeground information is more effective as a direct input than as auxiliary MetaQuery supervision. This advantage is clearest when native causal attention is preserved.

04

Distillation targets: let teachers keep reading original images

Starting point
N2 · Reviewed SAM main-view input
Change
The policy reads SAM images, while depth/video teachers read synchronized original images; foreground regions receive greater weight.

After replacing the main view, we revisit the model's depth/video distillation. The policy and teachers originally shared the processed images, but dimming and outlines also shift the teachers' input distribution. We therefore supply synchronized original images to the teachers while keeping SAM images as policy inputs.

Raw and masked images share the same augmentation parameters. The alignment loss is weighted by each patch's foreground fraction to focus supervision on task-relevant regions.

SAM main view + two wrist views
↔
Raw image → Depth / Video teacher

Randomized success improves by 2.3 points with background brightness at ×0.1 and by 3.9 points with a fully black background. The consistent improvement in both settings leads us to retain the combination of original-image teacher inputs and foreground weighting.

TakeawaySeparate inputs for the policy and teachers preserve the benefits of foreground processing while improving distillation supervision, without adding teacher overhead at inference.

04.a

A depth view: does explicit geometry help?

Starting point
N3 · SAM main view and original-image teachers
Change
Append a pseudo-color depth image, share the ViT, and use a separate depth merger.

After restoring the teachers' inputs, we try supplying geometry explicitly to the policy. We convert LingBot-Depth outputs into inverse-depth pseudo-color images as a fourth input, with a separate connector initialized from the RGB merger.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Three-view model · N315k5076.553.1
Depth map + separate connector15k5077.748.2
Depth map + separate connector20k5080.649.8

At 15k, the depth approach is slightly better on Clean, but achieves only 48.2% on Randomized—about 5 points below the three-view approach. At 20k, it still does not exceed the corresponding three-view result. Under the current training budget, the extra geometry input does not deliver the expected benefit.

One possible explanation is that a depth map is not well suited to being encoded as an independent image by the visual encoder and passed into the LLM. Depth information may work better as alignment supervision, allowing the model to learn geometric structure during training.

TakeawayRetain three visual inputs, with geometry continuing to contribute through distillation targets.

04.b

Global learning rate: lowering everything does not help

Starting point
N3 · Original-image teachers and foreground weighting
Change
Shorten the schedule to 30k; compare faster decay and a lower initial learning rate.

Beyond input processing, we also examine optimization. LingBot-VLA 2.0's default learning rate decays from 1e−4 to 5e−5 over 50k steps. We consider this relatively high for post-training, so our experiments focus on reducing it: first by decaying to a lower endpoint within 30k steps, and then by also lowering the initial rate.

05

Module-wise learning rates: update pretrained representations less

Starting point

Change
Lower learning rates for the ViT, visual merger, and LLM; freeze token embeddings.

Vision, language, and action modules have different roles and different pretraining histories. We want the vision-language modules to preserve more of their existing representations while allowing action and alignment modules to keep adapting to the downstream tasks. We therefore assign different learning-rate multipliers to each module.

05.a

Wrist augmentation: no consistent benefit from color perturbations

Starting point
N4 · Module-wise learning rates
Change
Apply photometric and color augmentations to the two wrist-camera images during training only.

With foreground processing already applied to the main view, the remaining appearance differences may come from the wrist cameras. We set augmentation ranges using lighting statistics from randomized scenes and perturb brightness, contrast, saturation, hue, gamma, and noise. Both wrist cameras share the same sampled lighting perturbation.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
No wrist augmentation · N415k5078.255.4

Randomized success does not improve at 15k or 25k, although at 20k it rises from 53.8% to 55.8%. Results vary across checkpoints, and Clean performance also declines. We do not observe a clear, consistent benefit.

By this stage, the preliminary-round deadline was approaching, so we chose to disable wrist augmentation. We cannot rule out that more training would have been needed to realize its benefits.

TakeawayDisable wrist color augmentation in the final recipe.

05.b

Task sampling: train more on difficult tasks

Starting point
N4 · Continue from the 25k checkpoint
Change
Set task-sampling probabilities from per-task failure rates; sample frames within each task without replacement.

Some tasks consistently lag behind the overall average. We try increasing their sampling probabilities: weights are constructed from the 25k model's mean failure rate across the two scenes, plus ε=0.05. Training samples a task first and then a frame.

ConfigurationStepEp / taskClean (%) ↑Random (%) ↑
Standard sampling · N425k5080.655.2
Task-weighted sampling30k5080.456.7
Standard sampling · N435k5080.556.2
Task-weighted sampling35k5079.854.6

Starting from N4 at 25k with standard sampling, task-weighted continuation to 30k raises Randomized success from 55.2% to 56.7%, a clear gain of about 1.5 percentage points. Clean falls slightly from 80.6% to 80.4%. Without a standard-sampling control at 30k, however, we cannot attribute this improvement entirely to the sampling strategy.

At 35k, standard sampling achieves 56.2% on Randomized, exceeding task-weighted sampling's 54.6%, and also performs better on Clean. Task-weighted continuation may already have overtrained after 10k additional steps from the 25k checkpoint; alternatively, the strategy itself may be ineffective. We did not investigate further because time was limited and the competition explicitly prohibited this kind of adjustment to task sampling based on evaluation feedback.

TakeawayRetain standard sampling in the final recipe.

06

Data repair: exclude padding and restore frame alignment

Starting point
N4 · Module-wise learning rates, without wrist augmentation or task-weighted sampling
Change
Exclude padded actions from the loss, repair video–action alignment, and regenerate SAM inputs.

Poor performance on click tasks prompted us to re-examine the training supervision. We identified two issues.

Padded actions were included in supervision

When fewer than 50 actions remain at the end of an episode, the last action is repeated to fill the chunk. The original loss supervises these padded positions too, potentially overemphasizing the final hold action. We combine a padding mask with the valid-joint mask to exclude padded positions from both the loss numerator and its normalization denominator.

Video frames and action trajectories were misaligned

Some video segments are shorter than their corresponding numeric trajectories, so frame lookup can cross episode boundaries or become misaligned with actions. We rebuild the frame-aligned training data, regenerate SAM inputs, and add frame-boundary checks.

Joint repair · N525k10082.056.2
Final model · N530k10081.958.2
Joint repair · N540k5083.757.7

At 20k, with 50 evaluation episodes per task in both settings, Randomized success rises from 53.8% to 57.0%, a gain of 3.2 percentage points; Clean falls from 80.9% to 78.9%. After training to 30k, the final model reaches Clean 81.86% and Randomized 58.22%, with an average success rate of 70.04%.

Compared with N4 before repair, click_bell and click_alarmclock improve particularly strongly. The training supervision deserves scrutiny alongside the training budget.

Both repairs were introduced together and have not been ablated separately. The chart below compares N4 before repair (25k, module-wise learning rates) and N5 after joint repair (25k), evaluated with 50 and 100 episodes, respectively, for each task in each scene.

TakeawayForeground processing, original-image teachers, module-wise learning rates, and data repairs together form our final recipe.

Conclusions

  1. Make new information directly available at the input

    Starting from the same original-image baseline, a fourth SAM view with causal attention outperforms auxiliary MetaQuery supervision. Replacing the main view with the foreground image works better still. On these tasks, making foreground information directly available during action prediction translates into manipulation gains more readily than shaping representations through a mask-reconstruction objective alone. When adding task-relevant information to a VLA, prioritize whether the policy can use it directly at inference.

  2. Preserve native VLM attention when adding inputs

    In the fourth-view experiments, the three positional encodings differ by only about 1.3 percentage points under causal attention. Switching to pair attention with the same encoding consistently reduces success by 2.6–5.0 points. New tokens add information, but they can also change how a pretrained model exchanges it. Before refining positional encodings for new content, first preserve the token-visibility relationships of the VLM's native causal attention.

  3. Balance retention and adaptation with module-wise learning rates

    Uniformly lowering the learning rate does not help. Lowering the rates for the ViT, visual merger, and LLM, freezing token embeddings, and retaining the update scale for action and alignment modules instead improves Randomized success by about 2.2 percentage points at both 15k and 25k. Modules need not change at the same rate during post-training: extensively pretrained modules whose representations we want to retain should use lower learning rates, or be frozen when appropriate, while modules responsible for downstream adaptation need sufficient room to update.

  4. Exclude padded actions from task supervision

    Padding is an artificial device for making action chunks the same length, not part of the demonstrated decision trajectory. For a VLA without memory or history in RoboTwin, repeatedly supervising end-of-episode hold actions may associate similar current observations with both continuing execution and remaining still. This can amplify ambiguity between a task that is still in progress and one that has finished. Padded actions should therefore be excluded from both the loss and its normalization denominator, so the model learns only from valid actions.

  5. Turn perception-model generalization into visual guidance for a VLA

    The ability of existing VLMs and video segmentation models to locate objects and extract foreground regions across scenes can provide effective guidance to a VLA through visual prompts. Our Qwen-SAM pipeline uses Qwen to interpret the instruction and identify relevant objects, then SAM to extract the foreground. In RoboTwin's clean-to-randomized setting, where the shift is primarily in scene appearance, SAM multi foreground inputs raise Randomized success from 36.2% to 47.8%; mask review and rendering adjustments bring it to 50.8%. These experiments demonstrate the pipeline's effectiveness in this transfer setting and offer a concrete way to connect System 1 and System 2 through visual prompts.
